title: dbt and analytics engineering
summary: A complete SQL-first route from real Core/DuckDB project files through tests, macros, snapshots, incremental correctness, contracts, documentation, targets, state/defer CI, governance and accepted data-product recovery.

units.title: A real dbt project and its execution stages
units.outcome: Build and inspect a local dbt project through its real adapter.
units.theory:
dbt transforms data by executing project-defined SQL through a database adapter. A project contains model files, configuration, tests and dependency declarations. A profile tells the adapter which owned database and execution settings to use. The classroom examples write ordinary project files into a temporary directory, invoke the installed dbt CLI through its Python interface and inspect a real DuckDB database. They do not simulate a dbt run.

Parsing, compilation and execution establish different facts. Parsing builds a graph and checks project structure. Compilation resolves template expressions into SQL. Running materializes model relations in the database. Building also includes selected tests and other dependency-aware resources. A compiled SQL file is therefore useful evidence of what would be submitted, but it does not prove that the relation exists or that its contents passed tests.

The Python wrapper is necessary because the classroom has one Python pad. Its file writes are explicit and local; you can inspect the normal dbt filenames in the source. An external multi-file project uses the same concepts, but persistence, credentials and orchestration require their own owned setup. Nothing in this lesson selects a cloud warehouse or installs packages while running.
units.syntax: dbt_project.yml declares the project name, version, profile name and resource directories. profiles.yml declares the local DuckDB path and bounded threading settings. Model SQL belongs under models/. dbtRunner.invoke receives a list of CLI arguments; calls run serially in this program. The result's success flag is checked before interpreting artifacts, and the database is queried independently after execution.

worked.title: Parse and build an actual relation
worked.explanation: The first case parses a one-model project, checks its manifest node, builds the model and queries the resulting relation. The answer 42 is verified in DuckDB rather than inferred from the source text. The run-results artifact is then checked for successful materialization.
worked.expected: A manifest node exists, the database returns 42, and the run result reports success.

worked.title: Compilation does not substitute for execution
worked.explanation: The second case inspects compiled SQL before running the model. It checks that no answer relation has yet been materialized, then runs the model and observes the result. The fixture deliberately computes the same answer through an expression.
worked.expected: Compiled SQL contains 6*7; the answer relation appears only after run.

exercises.title: Locate the project
exercises.task: Identify the model, project and profile files created by the wrapper.
exercises.check: Each file has a distinct responsibility.
exercises.hint: Read the project helper before the model.
exercises.answer: The model states SQL logic, project configuration defines resource locations, and the profile chooses the database. Keeping these roles separate prevents accidental environment assumptions.

exercises.title: Change the expression
exercises.task: Return 21*2 from the model and run it.
exercises.check: The database still returns 42.
exercises.hint: Inspect compiled SQL as well as output.
exercises.answer: The source expression changes while the result remains equal. That is a concrete example of why source identity and result equality are different evidence.

exercises.title: Introduce invalid SQL
exercises.task: Remove part of the select expression and observe the failed command.
exercises.check: Execution reports failure with a database diagnostic.
exercises.hint: Check the returned success value.
exercises.answer: Do not continue publication after a failed command. Preserve the diagnostic and distinguish parsing/template errors from SQL execution errors.

exercises.title: Inspect the manifest
exercises.task: Find the model's unique_id and original file path.
exercises.check: They identify the project node and source.
exercises.hint: Open target/manifest.json.
exercises.answer: The manifest is a structured graph artifact, not merely a log. It can support lineage and selection, but does not prove data quality by itself.

exercises.title: Inspect run results
exercises.task: Find status and execution information after build.
exercises.check: A successful model result is recorded.
exercises.hint: Read the actual output artifact.
exercises.answer: The result concerns this invocation and selected resources. A prior successful artifact should not be reused as evidence for changed source.

exercises.title: State the runtime boundary
exercises.task: Explain which files remain after the classroom job.
exercises.check: Source and bounded results remain; scratch project databases do not.
exercises.hint: The pad runs in a fresh job directory.
exercises.answer: For a durable external project, prepare an owned work directory and explicit database/artifact storage. Do not assume a temporary classroom path is a deployment.

units.diagnosis: A missing profile error usually means the project profile name and profiles.yml key disagree. A missing relation after compile is expected unless the model was run. A successful run with no tests is not a quality certificate. Inspect the command, selected resources, result status and actual database contents before deciding what was established.
units.transfer: Build and inspect a local dbt project through its real adapter. Keep parsing, compilation, materialization and validation distinct. This gives you a reliable basis for the later incremental, contract and publication lessons without depending on a hosted warehouse.

units.title: Seeds, staging and rejected records
units.outcome: Create a staging boundary with complete record accounting.
units.theory:
A seed is a small versioned CSV resource loaded by dbt. It is useful for fixtures and stable reference data; it is not a general replacement for an ingestion system. A staging model then gives source fields deliberate names and types. These are separate boundaries: loading records establishes that they reached a relation, while staging defines how the analysis interprets them.

The first case loads three amounts and verifies their total after staging. The second introduces a malformed token and uses a deliberate permissive conversion with a rejection condition. The raw relation remains available, so accepted rows can be reconciled with the original input. A cleaned table alone would hide the missing contribution and its cause.

A staging layer should preserve enough identity to explain every decision. Do not silently convert bad text to zero or drop an identifier to make a model pass. For a production source, include an ingestion identity, schema version and rejection reason; the classroom fixture keeps the data small enough to inspect directly.
units.syntax: CSV files belong under seeds/ and are referenced with ref just like dependency-aware relations. A staging model can use explicit casts for mandatory fields and try_cast when a null result is part of a declared rejection policy. The SQL WHERE condition decides which records enter the accepted relation. Compare accepted and rejected counts against the raw seed relation.

worked.title: Load and stage numeric records
worked.explanation: The first project builds a seed and its dependent staging model, then queries the actual result. Explicit integer casts make the output contract visible. The manifest also confirms that the input is a seed resource.
worked.expected: Three rows materialize and amount totals 21.

worked.title: Preserve a malformed input for diagnosis
worked.explanation: The second case keeps the raw relation while accepting only successfully parsed amounts. The bad token's record is counted independently, so it cannot disappear from the accounting.
worked.expected: Two rows are accepted, one is rejected, and all three remain in raw input.

exercises.title: Add a valid row
exercises.task: Add id 4 with amount 3 and rebuild.
exercises.check: Accepted total becomes 24.
exercises.hint: Predict the new contribution.
exercises.answer: The source and staged counts should both increase by one. Keep the identifier unique and verify the new row separately.

exercises.title: Add missing text
exercises.task: Add a blank amount and decide its category.
exercises.check: The policy distinguishes missing from malformed.
exercises.hint: A null parse result has more than one possible cause.
exercises.answer: Keep a raw-is-null or blank indicator and a rejection reason. Treating all failed conversions alike can hide different operational problems.

exercises.title: Keep the source identity
exercises.task: Return id alongside parsed amount.
exercises.check: Each accepted result can be traced to a raw record.
exercises.hint: Do not aggregate before accounting.
exercises.answer: Row identity supports diagnosis and later deduplication. A total without identifiers is insufficient to explain rejection.

exercises.title: Check source coverage
exercises.task: Count accepted and rejected records.
exercises.check: Their sum equals the raw count under the fixture policy.
exercises.hint: Make categories disjoint.
exercises.answer: The reconciliation fails if a row is counted twice or disappears. State classification order when duplicate and invalid conditions overlap.

exercises.title: Choose a seed use case
exercises.task: Explain whether daily production transactions should normally be manually maintained as a seed.
exercises.check: The answer distinguishes small reference data from ingestion.
exercises.hint: A versioned CSV has a limited role.
exercises.answer: Use seeds for small controlled fixtures or mappings. Production ingestion needs a separate reproducible source contract and operational process.

exercises.title: Fail mandatory parsing
exercises.task: Replace the permissive conversion with a strict cast.
exercises.check: The malformed fixture fails.
exercises.hint: This is an explicit policy choice.
exercises.answer: Use strict failure when invalid input must block the product. Keep the failed evidence and do not mistake a stopped run for data that never arrived.

units.diagnosis: A seed can load successfully while a staging cast fails. Conversely, permissive SQL can succeed while excluding important records. Inspect the raw relation, parsed field and rejection count. Do not repair an error by silently widening every field to text or swallowing all conversion failures.
units.transfer: Create a staging boundary with complete record accounting. State which invalid inputs block publication and which are quarantined, then test both paths using identified records. The same contract will later protect model features from silent data changes.

sql_variant.explanation: The SQL reference keeps paid orders 1, 2 and 5 with amounts 100, 50 and 120. Their total is 270. Removing the status filter returns the five-row population. units.title: Dependency graphs and materialization choices
units.outcome: Choose a materialization using observed database behavior and a stated workload.
units.theory:
ref creates a dependency on another dbt resource and resolves its database relation. That gives dbt a graph it can order and inspect. Hardcoding a table name can bypass this dependency information even when the SQL happens to run. The graph is therefore part of the execution contract, not just a diagram for documentation.

A materialization defines how a model result is represented. A view stores a query definition, a table stores a materialized result, and an ephemeral model is compiled into a dependent query rather than created as its own relation. These choices change storage, freshness, reuse and query cost. They do not change the need to validate grain and values.

The first case uses a staging view and a downstream table, then inspects both the manifest dependency and the actual database relation types. The second uses an ephemeral model to make the absence of a standalone relation explicit. The purpose is to connect configuration to observed behavior rather than memorize names.
units.syntax: config(materialized='view') or config(materialized='table') declares a model representation. ref('staging') connects the downstream model to its dependency. For an ephemeral input, compiled SQL includes a generated common-table expression. Inspect manifest depends_on nodes and information_schema tables to distinguish graph structure from database objects.

worked.title: Observe the graph and physical objects
worked.explanation: The first project links a seed to a staging view and then a materialized total. It verifies the manifest edge, the result 12 and the database object kinds. These checks answer complementary questions.
worked.expected: staging is a view, customer_total is a table, and its dependency names staging.

worked.title: Inspect an inlined ephemeral model
worked.explanation: The second case builds a dependent model that uses an ephemeral constant. The value reaches the final relation, but the ephemeral model itself is absent from the database object list.
worked.expected: The final answer is 42 and no base relation is created.

exercises.title: Remove a declared edge
exercises.task: Replace ref with a hardcoded relation name and inspect the manifest.
exercises.check: The explicit dependency disappears.
exercises.hint: SQL name resolution is not graph declaration.
exercises.answer: The query may still run if the relation already exists, but build ordering and state selection lose the declared relationship.

exercises.title: Change a representation
exercises.task: Switch staging from view to table and rebuild.
exercises.check: The observed relation type changes.
exercises.hint: Check information_schema.
exercises.answer: The change affects when data is recomputed and how much storage is used. It should be reviewed against freshness and downstream workload requirements.

exercises.title: Inspect compiled SQL
exercises.task: Locate the generated CTE for the ephemeral model.
exercises.check: The dependent query includes the base logic.
exercises.hint: No standalone base table is expected.
exercises.answer: Ephemeral reuse can duplicate logic across consumers. It is a design choice, not a universal performance optimization.

exercises.title: Add a downstream model
exercises.task: Create a second consumer using ref.
exercises.check: The graph contains its new edge.
exercises.hint: Name the dependency through the API.
exercises.answer: Test the result and review the graph. A valid edge does not establish the consumer's business semantics.

exercises.title: Compare freshness
exercises.task: Explain how a view and a table may expose changes in their upstream data.
exercises.check: The answer distinguishes query-time evaluation from materialization time.
exercises.hint: Inspect the stored representation.
exercises.answer: The exact behavior depends on the database and relation. A table usually requires another run to refresh its contents; a view evaluates its stored query when queried.

exercises.title: Choose a cost experiment
exercises.task: Design a fair comparison of two materializations.
exercises.check: Both satisfy the same values and freshness contract.
exercises.hint: Include refresh and read costs.
exercises.answer: Measure representative reads, build time and storage under the required freshness. Comparing one cached read alone would be incomplete.

units.diagnosis: A relation-not-found error can come from a missing graph edge or an unbuilt dependency. An absent ephemeral relation is expected. A fast view query on tiny data does not establish production performance. Inspect compilation and actual object types before changing orchestration order.
units.transfer: Choose a materialization using observed database behavior and a stated workload. Retain ref-based dependencies and test the resulting graph, values and freshness expectations. This supports reliable selection and deployment when the project grows.

units.title: Data tests and the meaning of a failed build
units.outcome: Use data tests as explicit evidence for a declared contract.
units.theory:
Data tests express conditions that a relation should satisfy. A not-null test checks presence, while a unique test checks a key candidate. They are useful safeguards, but passing them does not prove that every value is correct. A table can have unique identifiers and still use the wrong currency, time window or join.

A build can materialize a model before a test fails. That is an important operational boundary: detecting a bad result is different from preventing every consumer from seeing it. The second case deliberately creates duplicate identifiers, observes a failed test and verifies that the relation still exists. A later publication gate will use successful test artifacts to decide whether to expose a product.

Failure recovery should preserve the cause. Correct the fixture or transformation under a stated contract, rerun the required resources and inspect new results. Do not change a uniqueness test into a row-count test merely to obtain a green status. The expected key is part of the data model.
units.syntax: Model column metadata can declare data_tests such as not_null and unique. build includes selected tests in dependency order. target/run_results.json records statuses for the invocation. Check the returned success value and each relevant result; a model status success can coexist with a test status fail in the same build.

worked.title: Pass two independent key conditions
worked.explanation: The first case builds a two-row table and checks that both not-null and uniqueness tests pass. It also queries the row count directly. The program does not infer data quality solely from process exit.
worked.expected: Two test results pass and the table contains two rows.

worked.title: Observe failure and repair
worked.explanation: The duplicate fixture fails uniqueness while leaving a materialized table. The program then changes the second identifier, rebuilds and checks new success/pass statuses. The first failure remains an explicit part of the investigation.
worked.expected: Duplicate data is rejected by the test; the corrected rebuild passes.

exercises.title: Create a null key
exercises.task: Add a record with an absent identifier.
exercises.check: The not-null test fails.
exercises.hint: Uniqueness and presence are different conditions.
exercises.answer: Keep both tests when the contract requires a mandatory unique key. One cannot stand in for the other.

exercises.title: Keep duplicate payloads
exercises.task: Use two equal rows with the same id and amount.
exercises.check: Uniqueness still fails.
exercises.hint: Identical content does not make two rows one record.
exercises.answer: A deduplication policy may legitimately collapse retries upstream, but the model must apply that policy explicitly before claiming unique grain.

exercises.title: Inspect failure artifacts
exercises.task: Find the failed test identifier in run_results.
exercises.check: The artifact names the failing condition.
exercises.hint: Do not inspect only the final console line.
exercises.answer: Retain invocation identity and source version alongside the test result. A stale artifact from an earlier run is not current evidence.

exercises.title: Check materialized state
exercises.task: Query the bad table after the failed build.
exercises.check: It still exists in this local case.
exercises.hint: Tests can run after materialization.
exercises.answer: A quality gate must be connected to publication or access control if invalid output must remain unavailable to consumers.

exercises.title: Repair the contract
exercises.task: Fix the source identity and rerun the build.
exercises.check: Both tests pass on new evidence.
exercises.hint: Do not weaken the requirement.
exercises.answer: The correction should explain why the identifier is now valid. Renaming a duplicate arbitrarily would only conceal an unresolved identity problem.

exercises.title: Add a quantity check
exercises.task: Propose a test that key checks would miss.
exercises.check: It checks a meaningful domain or reconciliation rule.
exercises.hint: Unique rows can still have wrong totals.
exercises.answer: Use a signed amount rule, a source-total reconciliation or a declared accepted-value domain as appropriate. Every additional test needs a business meaning.

units.diagnosis: When a build fails, distinguish compilation, model execution and test failure. Check which relations were already materialized and whether publication was blocked. Avoid treating warning severity as an automatic acceptable outcome; it should follow a reviewed policy, not a desire for successful status.
units.transfer: Use data tests as explicit evidence for a declared contract. Demonstrate a known violation, inspect the materialized state and repair the source or transformation without weakening the assertion. Carry test outcomes into the later publication decision.

units.title: Source freshness and clock assumptions
units.outcome: Define and test a source freshness policy with an explicit clock and response.
units.theory:
Freshness asks whether a source has been updated within a permitted age. It is different from completeness, correctness and event-time coverage. A source can contain a recent timestamp while missing many records, and an old historical dataset can be complete for its intended purpose. Choose the freshness clock and threshold from the consumer's requirement.

The example uses the actual DuckDB clock and constructs a fresh record or a record two days old. A one-hour error threshold distinguishes those cases. The timestamp is explicitly timezone-aware. This is a bounded local check of dbt's freshness behavior, not an observation about an external ingestion service.

The meaning of loaded_at matters. It might represent ingestion completion, upstream publication or a field supplied by the source. If future timestamps, partial loads or clock skew are possible, max(loaded_at) alone can produce a misleading pass. A production contract should combine freshness with coverage, batch identity and relevant consistency checks.
units.syntax: A source declaration names a schema and table identifier independently of a model. Its loaded_at_field and freshness thresholds define the check. source freshness writes target/sources.json. The program checks its actual pass/error status and uses source() in the model to declare the dependency. Do not confuse this artifact with ordinary model run_results.

worked.title: Check a fresh local source
worked.explanation: The first case writes a timestamp near the current UTC time, loads the seed and runs the real freshness command. Its small timing margin is well inside the declared one-hour threshold.
worked.expected: The source freshness status is pass.

worked.title: Reject a stale source
worked.explanation: The second case subtracts two days from the same clock policy. The command is expected to fail under the one-hour threshold, and the sources artifact must record error. This is a designed negative case, not a swallowed unexpected failure.
worked.expected: The stale source reports error.

exercises.title: Change the threshold
exercises.task: Allow three days for the deliberately old source.
exercises.check: A two-day-old source can pass that revised policy.
exercises.hint: Thresholds encode a requirement.
exercises.answer: The outcome changes because the policy changed. Document who accepts that age and what decisions use the data.

exercises.title: Use a future timestamp
exercises.task: Describe how a future loaded_at value can mislead an age check.
exercises.check: The answer calls for a separate future-time validation.
exercises.hint: A recent maximum can hide bad clocks.
exercises.answer: Reject or investigate impossible future timestamps within a declared skew tolerance. A negative age is not evidence of a healthy ingestion process.

exercises.title: Separate event and load time
exercises.task: Give an old event a recent ingestion timestamp.
exercises.check: Fresh ingestion does not imply recent event coverage.
exercises.hint: There are two different clocks.
exercises.answer: Check event-time coverage separately when the consumer needs a recent event window. Late arrivals can be valid under the ingestion contract.

exercises.title: Inspect the artifact
exercises.task: Read sources.json and identify the tested source.
exercises.check: The source identifier and status are retained.
exercises.hint: This command has a distinct artifact.
exercises.answer: Record the invocation and exact threshold with the result. A status without its policy is difficult to interpret.

exercises.title: Test partial ingestion
exercises.task: Explain why one recent row cannot prove a complete batch.
exercises.check: The answer names a coverage or batch-integrity check.
exercises.hint: max alone ignores missing rows.
exercises.answer: Use expected partitions, counts, batch manifests or other source-specific reconciliation. Combine independent dimensions of reliability.

exercises.title: Define an action
exercises.task: Specify what happens when freshness fails.
exercises.check: The action distinguishes blocking, fallback and investigation.
exercises.hint: A diagnostic needs an operational response.
exercises.answer: For a critical feature, the consumer might refuse publication or use an explicitly valid older model/input. Record the degraded state rather than silently using stale values.

units.diagnosis: A stale-source error can be correct behavior under the declared threshold. Check timestamp parsing, timezone, clock skew and the meaning of loaded_at before increasing the limit. If the source passes but users see missing data, investigate completeness rather than claiming freshness proved everything.
units.transfer: Define and test a source freshness policy with an explicit clock and response. Pair it with batch completeness and time-coverage checks appropriate to the consumer. Keep the local fixture evidence separate from claims about an actual upstream service.

units.title: Unit fixtures and integration tests
units.outcome: Use controlled fixtures to test transformation logic and real-data checks to test integration.
units.theory:
A unit fixture supplies controlled inputs to test a model's transformation logic. An integration test examines relations produced from an actual source or seed. Both are useful, but they answer different questions. A unit fixture can demonstrate aggregation behavior on a boundary case without claiming that the production input has valid keys or complete coverage.

The worked model sums amounts per customer. Its unit fixture contains two orders for one customer, while the actual loaded seed contains a different customer and amount. The expected result belongs to the fixture, not to the seed. Checking that the seed remains unchanged makes the distinction concrete.

The second case deliberately uses the wrong expected total. dbt must report a failed unit test even though the SQL is executable. A test suite should contain examples that would fail under meaningful defects such as missing grouping, wrong keys, incorrect boundaries or duplicated joins. Tests that only repeat the model's own calculation can agree with the same mistake.
units.syntax: The unit_tests YAML section names the model, supplied inputs and expected rows. The input declaration ref('raw_orders') substitutes a controlled relation for that dependency. The example first prepares the parent schema, then selects test_type:unit. Result artifacts are inspected for the actual pass or fail status.

worked.title: Use a controlled unit population
worked.explanation: The fixture amounts 2 and 3 belong to customer 1 and should sum to 5. The loaded source amount 100 belongs to another row and is not used as the fixture expectation. The program verifies that the underlying seed remains 100.
worked.expected: The unit test passes with total 5 and the source seed is unchanged.

worked.title: Require a wrong expectation to fail
worked.explanation: The second case changes only the expected total to 99. A robust test runner should reject that expectation rather than infer success from SQL compilation or an available model relation.
worked.expected: The unit result is fail under the incorrect expected row.

exercises.title: Add a second customer
exercises.task: Supply a fixture with two customer groups.
exercises.check: The expected result has one row per customer.
exercises.hint: Make the grouping key observable.
exercises.answer: This catches a model that returns one global total. Verify row identities as well as amounts.

exercises.title: Add a zero amount
exercises.task: Include a zero-valued order for an existing customer.
exercises.check: The total is unchanged but row coverage increases.
exercises.hint: Some defects do not change additive totals.
exercises.answer: A separate count output or row-accounting test can reveal a dropped zero-valued row when that distinction matters.

exercises.title: Change a key
exercises.task: Use two distinct customer identifiers with the same display label.
exercises.check: They remain separate groups.
exercises.hint: Identity is not a label.
exercises.answer: The fixture should catch grouping by a nonunique display field. Use the actual intended key in both SQL and expectation.

exercises.title: Remove a grouping clause
exercises.task: Introduce a transformation defect and observe failure.
exercises.check: The unit test rejects wrong output or SQL.
exercises.hint: Tests need a meaningful counterexample.
exercises.answer: A failure proves that this fixture detects that defect. It does not prove the suite detects all possible changes.

exercises.title: Compare test types
exercises.task: Explain what the unit fixture cannot establish about the source.
exercises.check: It cannot prove actual source completeness or uniqueness.
exercises.hint: Synthetic inputs have controlled properties.
exercises.answer: Use integration tests, source contracts and operational observations for the actual data. Keep the evidence categories separate.

exercises.title: Build an independent oracle
exercises.task: Calculate expected totals directly from the small input rows.
exercises.check: The oracle does not copy the SQL expression verbatim.
exercises.hint: Use transparent arithmetic or a different implementation.
exercises.answer: Independent expected values reduce the risk that the model and test share the same error. Document the assumptions behind the oracle.

units.diagnosis: An empty selected test set is not a passing unit test. Check how many results were returned and their identifiers. Schema preparation errors should be distinguished from a wrong expected row. Do not change expected output merely because the current implementation produced something else.
units.transfer: Use controlled fixtures to test transformation logic and real-data checks to test integration. Include at least one counterexample that would detect a plausible defect, and retain the source and expected rows needed to explain the result.

units.title: Jinja macros and compiled SQL evidence
units.outcome: Review a macro through its source, emitted SQL and actual result.
units.theory:
A dbt macro generates SQL during compilation. It can reduce repeated logic and centralize a reviewed calculation, but it is not a Python row function executed once for each database record. The generated SQL is what the database evaluates. Inspecting compiled SQL is therefore an important part of understanding and debugging a macro.

The ratio macro receives SQL expressions for a numerator and denominator. It emits a CASE expression that returns null for a zero denominator and performs floating division otherwise. That is a declared undefined-rate policy, not a universal rule. A different consumer might reject zero-trial groups or expose a separate status field. The macro should make the choice visible rather than hide it behind a convenient name.

Template arguments also have trust and quoting boundaries. A trusted model expression is different from an arbitrary user-supplied string. Reusing text in SQL does not automatically make it a safe identifier or a bound parameter. The lesson uses fixed authored expressions and an owned local database. External input needs a separately designed validation and parameterization boundary.
units.syntax: A macro is declared with Jinja macro/endmacro blocks and called inside double-brace expressions. The example's arguments are trusted column-expression strings. compile expands the macro into ordinary SQL; build then evaluates it. An undefined macro is a compilation error, which should be diagnosed before reasoning about database rows.

worked.title: Inspect a complete expansion
worked.explanation: The valid project generates rates for a normal count and a zero denominator. It checks actual values and reads compiled SQL to verify that the macro call has been expanded. Both the source abstraction and the executed expression remain inspectable.
worked.expected: The rates are 0.25 andnull; compiled SQL contains CASE logic rather than the macro call.

worked.title: Stop on an undefined abstraction
worked.explanation: The second case calls a macro that does not exist. The compiler must reject it and must not produce a successful compiled model file. This distinguishes a template-definition problem from a numeric result.
worked.expected: Compilation fails before model execution.

exercises.title: Change the zero policy
exercises.task: Return a separate invalid-denominator flag alongside the rate.
exercises.check: Zero-trial rows remain identifiable.
exercises.hint: A null value alone can have several causes.
exercises.answer: Publish both the rate and a named status or denominator. Consumers can then distinguish no observations from missing source counts.

exercises.title: Check integer behavior
exercises.task: Use 1 success and 4 trials and inspect the result type.
exercises.check: The rate is 0.25 rather than an integer truncation.
exercises.hint: Read the generated cast.
exercises.answer: The macro explicitly chooses floating division. Portability across adapters still needs testing because database type rules differ.

exercises.title: Review macro inputs
exercises.task: Explain why arbitrary user text should not become a SQL expression.
exercises.check: The answer identifies the trust boundary.
exercises.hint: Template substitution is not parameter binding.
exercises.answer: Validate identifiers and use appropriate binding for values in external interfaces. This classroom macro accepts fixed project-authored expressions only.

exercises.title: Inspect compiled code
exercises.task: Locate the CASE expression under target/compiled.
exercises.check: The generated expression is readable.
exercises.hint: The database does not execute the macro name.
exercises.answer: Review compilation when a macro changes. A short source call can hide a large semantic change in the emitted SQL.

exercises.title: Test a negative denominator
exercises.task: Define a policy for negative trial counts.
exercises.check: The policy explicitly rejects or classifies the invalid domain.
exercises.hint: Zero handling is not full domain validation.
exercises.answer: Add a data test or guard for the count domain. A mathematically computed negative rate does not make invalid counts acceptable.

exercises.title: Version shared logic
exercises.task: Describe what should be reviewed when the macro changes.
exercises.check: Affected consumers and their semantics are identified.
exercises.hint: A shared helper has a dependency surface.
exercises.answer: Inspect downstream models, tests, compiled SQL and compatibility requirements. A macro refactor should preserve the promised calculation or declare a versioned change.

units.diagnosis: If compilation fails, inspect macro discovery, names and argument syntax. If results are wrong, inspect the compiled SQL and numeric domain. Do not patch a macro by suppressing undefined names or replacing every exceptional denominator with zero. That can produce clean output while changing the analytical question.
units.transfer: Review a macro through its source, emitted SQL and actual result. Keep domain assumptions explicit and test contrasting numeric cases. Use abstraction to make a calculation consistent without hiding the evidence needed to validate it.

units.title: Incremental watermarks and late-arriving records
units.outcome: State the assumptions under which an incremental result equals a full recomputation.
units.theory:
An incremental model reuses an existing relation and processes selected new or changed records. This can reduce work, but it introduces state into the transformation. The result now depends on the previous materialization, the new source and the selection rule. A full recomputation and an incremental update should agree under the assumptions of that rule.

A strict maximum watermark is appropriate only when relevant records arrive with a monotonically increasing key and previously processed records do not change. The first case uses that narrow assumption and demonstrates a repeatable append. The second adds a record whose update key falls behind the current maximum. It is new to the pipeline but not newer under the chosen predicate, so it is missed.

The defect is not fixed by repeatedly running the same query. The program explicitly compares the incremental result with a full refresh to expose the missing record. A production strategy needs a late-arrival policy, a backfill process or a different source/change-tracking contract. Performance savings must be evaluated alongside those correctness assumptions.
units.syntax: config(materialized='incremental') declares the representation. is_incremental() identifies runs with an existing incremental relation, and this refers to that relation. The example selects source rows with updated_at greater than the target maximum. --full-refresh deliberately rebuilds the model; it is not the same operation as a normal rerun.

worked.title: A monotone append satisfies its assumptions
worked.explanation: The first case begins with one record, then adds a later key. A further run has no newer records and should not duplicate output. The database is checked after each complete sequence rather than assuming idempotency from the code shape.
worked.expected: Two records remain after the append and repeat run.

worked.title: A late record violates the watermark assumption
worked.explanation: The second case adds a record with key 15 after the target maximum reaches 20. The incremental predicate excludes it. A full refresh sees all three records, providing an independent comparison of the two execution paths.
worked.expected: The incremental relation has 2 rows; full refresh has 3.

exercises.title: Add a later event
exercises.task: Insert a record whose update key exceeds the watermark.
exercises.check: The incremental relation gains that record.
exercises.hint: Compare against the actual target maximum.
exercises.answer: The case demonstrates the intended append condition. Keep a stable identity so the inserted row can be verified.

exercises.title: Repeat without changes
exercises.task: Run the incremental model again with the same source.
exercises.check: No duplicate record appears under this fixture.
exercises.hint: The strict predicate selects no new rows.
exercises.answer: This is idempotency under the stated monotone append assumptions. It does not establish correct updates or late-data handling.

exercises.title: Add a late event
exercises.task: Insert a new id behind the current maximum.
exercises.check: The normal incremental result misses it.
exercises.hint: New to the pipeline differs from newer timestamp.
exercises.answer: Retain this counterexample and compare with a full recomputation. Do not describe a successful incremental run as complete without the arrival assumption.

exercises.title: Modify an old record
exercises.task: Change a previously loaded amount without changing its update key.
exercises.check: The simple append strategy does not reliably apply that correction.
exercises.hint: The predicate and write strategy both matter.
exercises.answer: Use a reviewed change indicator and keyed update/backfill strategy. A timestamp that does not change cannot communicate the correction.

exercises.title: Define a backfill
exercises.task: Specify a controlled way to recover missed history.
exercises.check: The scope and expected reconciliation are explicit.
exercises.hint: A full refresh is one possible bounded mechanism.
exercises.answer: For a large system, choose partitions or versioned replacement under an owned plan. Verify keys and totals before publishing the repaired result.

exercises.title: Compare costs fairly
exercises.task: Describe what an incremental performance claim must include.
exercises.check: It includes state maintenance and repair obligations.
exercises.hint: A cheap normal run is not the entire lifecycle.
exercises.answer: Account for late data, failures, backfills, validation and freshness requirements. Correctness boundaries should be part of the cost comparison.

units.diagnosis: If an incremental run succeeds but records are missing, inspect the target watermark and arrival pattern. If duplicates appear, inspect both the source predicate and write strategy. Keep an independently recomputed small fixture to detect divergence instead of relying only on the incremental table's own counts.
units.transfer: State the assumptions under which an incremental result equals a full recomputation. Test both a valid append and a late-arrival violation, then define the required repair or stronger strategy. The next lesson adds keyed updates with an explicit lookback bound.

units.title: Keyed updates, lookback windows and idempotency
units.outcome: Implement a keyed incremental contract with tested boundary and repeat-run behavior.
units.theory:
A keyed incremental strategy can replace records whose identity is already present. A lookback window can revisit recent source records so corrections and bounded late arrivals are considered. Together, these mechanisms address some weaknesses of a pure append watermark. They still require a valid key, deterministic source selection and a bound on lateness.

The example uses DuckDB's delete+insert strategy with id as the matching key. The source predicate includes a ten-unit lookback behind the current maximum. An update to id 1 and a late insertion of id 3 are therefore included, while unchanged id 2 can be revisited without creating another copy. The result is checked again after a repeat run.

The counterexample arrives outside that lookback. It remains missing until a full refresh. A ten-unit window is a data-contract choice, not proof that older corrections cannot occur. Also, unique_key configures incremental matching; it does not by itself replace a data test proving that the selected source has one record per key.
units.syntax: unique_key names the matching identity. incremental_strategy='delete+insert' is an adapter-specific implementation choice that must be supported by the prepared database. The lookback predicate uses >= so the lower boundary is included. Keep an independent uniqueness test and a reviewed policy for multiple source versions of the same key.

worked.title: Revisit rows without duplicating them
worked.explanation: The first case updates an existing amount and adds a late record within the allowed window. It then reruns the model to verify the same three identified values. This checks the combination of selection and write semantics.
worked.expected: Final amounts are id 1=6, id 2=7 and id 3=9, with three rows after rerun.

worked.title: Expose the limit of a finite lookback
worked.explanation: The second case adds a record older than the ten-unit window. A normal update misses it, while full refresh recovers it. The result makes the lateness assumption visible rather than describing lookback as universal correctness.
worked.expected: Normal output has 1 row; a declared full refresh produces 2.

exercises.title: Test the exact boundary
exercises.task: Add a record at max(updated_at)-10.
exercises.check: The inclusive predicate considers it.
exercises.hint: The operator is >=.
exercises.answer: Record whether the business policy includes that boundary and test it explicitly. A small operator change can alter historical coverage.

exercises.title: Repeat a correction
exercises.task: Apply the same corrected source twice.
exercises.check: The identified result remains unchanged.
exercises.hint: Check both values and row count.
exercises.answer: Idempotency requires deterministic selection and matching. Comparing only a total can miss offsetting duplicate and missing records.

exercises.title: Duplicate a source key
exercises.task: Add two selected records with one id.
exercises.check: A separate key test detects the ambiguity.
exercises.hint: unique_key is not an automatic source uniqueness guarantee.
exercises.answer: Resolve versions before the incremental write or fail the build. Arbitrary ordering can otherwise determine which state survives.

exercises.title: Widen the lookback
exercises.task: Include a previously missed old record by changing the window.
exercises.check: The record is selected under the revised policy.
exercises.hint: Measure added work as well as correctness.
exercises.answer: A wider window changes compute and still has a limit. Choose it from observed/contracted lateness and maintain a separate repair process.

exercises.title: Compare with full recomputation
exercises.task: Rebuild the small fixture and compare keyed rows.
exercises.check: The accepted incremental case matches.
exercises.hint: Use stable ordering and schema.
exercises.answer: This is a strong regression for the fixture. Production completeness still depends on the source versioning and arrival contract.

exercises.title: Specify a correction ledger
exercises.task: List what should be recorded for a backfill.
exercises.check: It includes identity, time scope, source version and reconciliation.
exercises.hint: A repair needs reproducible evidence.
exercises.answer: Retain the reason, affected keys or partitions, input version, old/new checks and publication decision. Do not silently rewrite historical outputs.

units.diagnosis: If a keyed update creates duplicates, inspect selected-source uniqueness rather than assuming unique_key enforced it. If old corrections are missed, inspect the lookback bound. If a rerun changes results without source changes, inspect ordering, nondeterministic expressions and external state.
units.transfer: Implement a keyed incremental contract with tested boundary and repeat-run behavior. Explain which late arrivals it accepts, which require repair and how the result is reconciled with a full recomputation. Keep the policy explicit as data volume grows.

units.title: Snapshots and observed historical state
units.outcome: Explain what a snapshot actually observed and what it cannot reconstruct.
units.theory:
A snapshot records changes in a mutable source as observed by successive snapshot runs. It can support slowly changing dimension history, but it cannot recover states that were never observed between runs. Its validity intervals describe the snapshot's chosen strategy and clock. Those intervals should not automatically be treated as the true business-effective time of every change.

The example uses the check strategy to detect a change in region for a stable customer identifier. dbt stores a closed historical version and a current version. The second case also removes a customer from the source and uses hard_deletes='invalidate' so the previously current record is closed. Without a declared deletion policy, consumers can misinterpret missing source records.

History is meaningful only with a stable identity and clear column choices. A changed display name, a corrected attribute and a genuinely new entity are different events. Decide which changes create new versions and which time interpretation the downstream consumer requires.
units.syntax: The modern YAML snapshot declares a relation, unique_key, strategy, check_cols and deletion policy. The example obtains the actual relation name from the generated manifest because custom schema naming can depend on the adapter/profile. dbt_valid_to is null for current versions under this contract. Query both all historical rows and the active subset.

worked.title: Observe an attribute change
worked.explanation: The first case snapshots two customers, changes one region, and snapshots again. The history has three versions in total, with two current customers. The old region remains observable rather than being overwritten.
worked.expected: There are 3 history rows; current regions are west and south.

worked.title: Invalidate a deleted source entity
worked.explanation: The second case changes one customer and removes the other. The explicit deletion policy closes the removed customer's current version. It does not invent a new active customer or silently erase history.
worked.expected: History still has 3 rows, but only customer 1/west is current.

exercises.title: Inspect a closed version
exercises.task: Query the old region and its validity endpoint.
exercises.check: The changed version has a non-null dbt_valid_to.
exercises.hint: Current and historical predicates differ.
exercises.answer: Retain both versions and their interval meaning. A current-only query is appropriate for a different question than a historical reconstruction.

exercises.title: Change a tracked column
exercises.task: Add another attribute to check_cols.
exercises.check: Its changes can create new versions under the revised policy.
exercises.hint: The tracked column set is part of the contract.
exercises.answer: Review whether the attribute represents meaningful state or noisy metadata. Tracking every field can produce unnecessary history churn.

exercises.title: Explain unobserved changes
exercises.task: Describe a source that changes twice between snapshot runs.
exercises.check: The intermediate state may never appear in the snapshot.
exercises.hint: Observation frequency limits evidence.
exercises.answer: Use a source change log or another stronger history mechanism when the intermediate state matters. Snapshots cannot reconstruct unobserved facts.

exercises.title: Compare deletion policies
exercises.task: Explain the effect of ignoring source deletions.
exercises.check: A formerly current record can remain open.
exercises.hint: Missing source data needs interpretation.
exercises.answer: Choose a policy that distinguishes genuine deletion from incomplete ingestion. A partial load should not automatically invalidate valid entities.

exercises.title: Review temporal meaning
exercises.task: Distinguish snapshot observation time from business-effective time.
exercises.check: The explanation keeps the clocks separate.
exercises.hint: The check strategy observes changes when it runs.
exercises.answer: For event-effective analyses, preserve source effective/known times and define a temporal model. Do not infer them from snapshot timing alone.

exercises.title: Verify identity
exercises.task: Add a source uniqueness test on customer_id.
exercises.check: Conflicting identity is detected before trusting history.
exercises.hint: A stable key is required.
exercises.answer: Multiple source rows for one snapshot key need a deterministic, justified resolution or a failure. Otherwise the historical record becomes ambiguous.

units.diagnosis: Unexpected history growth may come from unstable keys or noisy tracked columns. Unexpected open records may come from the deletion policy. A historical result can also be temporally wrong even when its interval columns are well-formed. Inspect source completeness and time semantics before changing snapshot configuration.
units.transfer: Explain what a snapshot actually observed and what it cannot reconstruct. Verify current and closed versions, define deletion handling, and preserve identity and clock contracts before using the history for features or analysis.

units.title: Enforced model schemas and constraint boundaries
units.outcome: Define a model schema contract and verify both accepted and rejected changes.
units.theory:
A model contract declares the output columns and types expected by consumers. Enforcing that contract can reject an incompatible model before a replacement relation is published. It complements data tests, which inspect conditions on resulting records. Schema compatibility and data quality remain different dimensions of a reliable product.

The first model declares an integer identifier and a bigint amount. Explicit SQL casts make the intended types predictable. The second case first builds a valid table, then changes amount into incompatible text. The command must fail, and the program checks that the previously valid relation remains available for this specific failure path.

That observation is deliberately narrow. It does not establish that an entire multi-model build is atomic or that every failure rolls back every prior change. Another model may have materialized earlier, and data tests can fail after materialization. Publication needs its own project-level decision and recovery contract.
units.syntax: The model config contains contract.enforced=true and a complete column/type declaration. Column constraints such as not_null depend on database support. An explicit cast documents the intended SQL type; it should not be used to hide a value-domain error. Query actual database contents after failure to establish what state survived.

worked.title: Create a compatible relation
worked.explanation: The valid model declares two fields and produces a matching row. The program checks actual values after build. The schema is a promise to a consumer, while the row assertion is evidence about this particular fixture.
worked.expected: The model returns id 1 and amount 42 under the declared types.

worked.title: Reject incompatible output
worked.explanation: The second case changes the amount expression to varchar. Contract validation rejects the altered output, and the previous amount 42 remains in the relation. The guide treats that result as a tested failure path rather than a universal transaction guarantee.
worked.expected: The incompatible run fails and the previous valid amount remains 42.

exercises.title: Remove a declared column
exercises.task: Delete amount from the model output.
exercises.check: The enforced contract rejects the mismatch.
exercises.hint: The declared schema is complete.
exercises.answer: A consumer cannot safely assume the missing field exists. Treat removal as a compatibility change rather than silently updating the contract.

exercises.title: Add a new output field
exercises.task: Add an undeclared field and inspect enforcement.
exercises.check: The schema change is explicit.
exercises.hint: More columns can still change a contract.
exercises.answer: Review the consumer interface and update/version the contract deliberately. Do not assume additional fields are harmless in every downstream system.

exercises.title: Test a null identifier
exercises.task: Return null for the constrained identifier.
exercises.check: The database/contract path reports the violation when supported.
exercises.hint: Schema type and value presence differ.
exercises.answer: Keep data tests as appropriate and inspect adapter constraint support. A declared constraint should not be advertised as enforced without actual evidence.

exercises.title: Distinguish failure stages
exercises.task: Compare the incompatible-schema case with the earlier uniqueness-test failure.
exercises.check: The two cases leave different observed state.
exercises.hint: Where validation occurs matters.
exercises.answer: A schema preflight may reject replacement earlier, while a data test can fail after materialization. Design publication around the actual sequence.

exercises.title: Check consumer assumptions
exercises.task: List properties beyond column types.
exercises.check: They include grain, units, time and missingness.
exercises.hint: An integer field can still mean the wrong thing.
exercises.answer: Add semantic contracts and tests. Schema enforcement does not establish that amount uses the expected currency or period.

exercises.title: Plan an incompatible change
exercises.task: Describe a safe way to replace gross amount with net amount.
exercises.check: It uses an explicit version and consumer migration.
exercises.hint: A type-preserving semantic change can still break users.
exercises.answer: Publish a new version with its definition, compare results, migrate consumers and retain rollback evidence. The next lesson makes version selection explicit.

units.diagnosis: A contract error may be the correct protection against an incompatible model. Inspect declared and actual column names/types instead of disabling enforcement. After failure, inspect the database and invocation artifacts; do not assume every relation reverted to a prior state.
units.transfer: Define a model schema contract and verify both accepted and rejected changes. Keep the observed failure timing separate from broader transaction claims, and combine structural compatibility with semantic and publication checks.

units.title: Model versions and semantic compatibility
units.outcome: Manage a semantic model change with explicit consumer versioning.
units.theory:
A model version identifies a particular contract. Consumers can reference an explicit version or follow the declared latest version. Those choices have different change behavior. An explicit version supports a controlled migration; following latest can be appropriate only when the consumer accepts the change policy.

The first case gives two versions the same column name and numeric type but different values. A stable consumer requests version 1 and receives 100, while an unversioned consumer follows version 2 and receives 80. This is intentionally a semantic change, not a parser or dtype error. A type-compatible change can still alter a model feature, dashboard metric or business decision.

The second case makes the meaning explicit: gross 100 minus returns 20 yields net 80. The dependency graph records where the calculation came from, but it does not decide whether a consumer intended gross or net. Versioning, descriptions, comparison evidence and a migration plan work together.
units.syntax: The model metadata declares latest_version and its versions, with defined_in pointing to the implementation files. ref('customer_value', version=1) selects an explicit contract. A plain ref follows the declared latest version. Inspect both the resolved database result and manifest dependency information.

worked.title: Resolve explicit and latest consumers
worked.explanation: The first project builds both versions and two consumers. Their results demonstrate the consequence of version selection while keeping the output type unchanged. The example avoids implying that a version number automatically guarantees compatibility.
worked.expected: The explicit v1 consumer returns 100; the latest v2 consumer returns 80.

worked.title: Name the semantic difference
worked.explanation: The second project computes a net quantity from its defined components and records the dependency edge. It provides enough meaning to explain why a consumer might need a different version or retraining.
worked.expected: Net is 80, derived from gross 100 and returns 20.

exercises.title: Pin a consumer
exercises.task: Change the latest consumer to request version 1 explicitly.
exercises.check: It returns 100.
exercises.hint: Use the version argument.
exercises.answer: Pinning defines the chosen contract. It also creates a responsibility to review and migrate deliberately when the old version is retired.

exercises.title: Change latest selection
exercises.task: Declare version 1 as latest in the fixture.
exercises.check: The unversioned consumer follows that declaration.
exercises.hint: Latest is project metadata.
exercises.answer: The behavior is controlled by configuration, not a universal semantic ordering. Keep release and consumer expectations explicit.

exercises.title: Add a type-compatible defect
exercises.task: Change the value while keeping the same type and name.
exercises.check: Schema checks alone can still pass.
exercises.hint: Meaning is not captured by dtype.
exercises.answer: Add semantic reconciliation and consumer-level checks. A feature can remain Float64 while changing units or time windows.

exercises.title: Design a model migration
exercises.task: Explain what a trained model needs when its input changes from gross to net.
exercises.check: The answer includes feature version and validation.
exercises.hint: The old coefficients were trained under a different meaning.
exercises.answer: Evaluate or retrain under the new feature contract, compare decisions and retain a rollback-compatible bundle. Do not change the upstream alias silently.

exercises.title: Inspect lineage
exercises.task: Find the dependency for the net model in the manifest.
exercises.check: It points to the declared base model.
exercises.hint: Lineage records a relationship.
exercises.answer: Use lineage to identify affected consumers. It does not itself prove that the calculation answers their intended question.

exercises.title: Retain rollback information
exercises.task: List the artifacts needed to restore a previous consumer contract.
exercises.check: They identify source, model version and validated data/interface.
exercises.hint: A version label alone is insufficient.
exercises.answer: Retain the implementation, dependency versions, schema/semantic definition and accepted evidence. A rollback should restore a coherent bundle.

units.diagnosis: If a result changes without a schema error, inspect semantic definitions and version resolution. An unversioned ref can follow a new latest contract intentionally. If a pinned consumer fails after removal of an old version, follow the migration policy instead of silently retargeting it.
units.transfer: Manage a semantic model change with explicit consumer versioning. Demonstrate the changed result, identify affected consumers and define validation and rollback requirements. Carry the same discipline into ML feature and model artifact versions.

units.title: Selectors, graph expansion and state comparison
units.outcome: Construct and inspect a reproducible selection against an explicit baseline.
units.theory:
Selection controls which resources a command considers. A tag-based selection expresses a group chosen by project metadata; graph operators expand to related resources. State selection compares current project metadata with a saved manifest. These mechanisms can reduce work, but they are not themselves tests of scientific correctness or deployment safety.

The first case tags a base model and selects it with its downstream dependent. The unrelated model is excluded. The second saves a manifest, changes one source file and uses state:modified+ to include the changed model and its downstream consumer. The selected set is inspected explicitly before any claim about reduced validation is made.

A state comparison depends on the baseline manifest. Keeping that baseline inside the directory that the next command overwrites can destroy the comparison. Save it separately with its source revision and environment identity. Also distinguish a changed definition from changed underlying data: a source can receive new records while the model file remains unchanged.
units.syntax: ls returns the selected resource list without running model transformations. tag:feature+ adds downstream graph expansion. state:modified+ compares definitions against --state and includes downstream resources. The program uses --resource-type model and --output name so its expected set is explicit. Keep state artifacts outside the active target output directory.

worked.title: Select a tagged subgraph
worked.explanation: The first project has a tagged base model, its child and an unrelated model. The actual list result must contain exactly base and child. This validates selection semantics without treating the selection as an executed data test.
worked.expected: The selected model names are base and child.

worked.title: Compare against a saved manifest
worked.explanation: The second case saves a prior manifest before editing base.sql. The state selector includes the modified base and its dependent child. The baseline remains separate from the command's new target artifacts.
worked.expected: Changed and downstream selection contains both models.

exercises.title: Remove graph expansion
exercises.task: Select tag:feature without the plus suffix.
exercises.check: Only the explicitly tagged model is selected.
exercises.hint: Tags and dependency traversal are different operations.
exercises.answer: Use graph operators deliberately and inspect the returned set. A tag on one model does not automatically label every downstream consumer.

exercises.title: Add an unrelated change
exercises.task: Edit the unrelated model and inspect state selection.
exercises.check: The changed node appears under the matching state selector.
exercises.hint: Compare with the saved manifest.
exercises.answer: Record the baseline revision and exact selection expression. The expected scope should be reviewed rather than inferred from a successful command.

exercises.title: Protect the baseline
exercises.task: Store prior manifest data outside target/.
exercises.check: The next invocation does not overwrite it.
exercises.hint: The active output directory is mutable.
exercises.answer: Use a dedicated state directory or immutable CI artifact. A self-overwritten baseline can incorrectly make changes appear absent.

exercises.title: Change only data
exercises.task: Explain why new source rows can matter without a model-file edit.
exercises.check: The answer distinguishes definitions from data state.
exercises.hint: state:modified is not a data freshness check.
exercises.answer: Use the selection appropriate to the data update and validate relevant outputs. Definition comparison alone cannot establish that existing materializations are current.

exercises.title: Inspect selected tests
exercises.task: Include tests and examine the resource types returned.
exercises.check: The intended tests are visible in the selection.
exercises.hint: Selecting models is not proof of test inclusion.
exercises.answer: Review indirect-selection policy and the actual result list. An empty test selection must not be reported as a successful validation suite.

exercises.title: Record a CI decision
exercises.task: List the evidence needed to justify a reduced build.
exercises.check: It includes baseline, selection, dependencies and executed results.
exercises.hint: A selection plan is only one stage.
exercises.answer: Keep the source revision, manifest identity, selected node set, commands and actual outcomes. Use a broader gate when the change affects shared semantics or operational assumptions.

units.diagnosis: Unexpectedly small selections can result from tags, graph direction, indirect-test rules or an overwritten baseline. Inspect ls output before executing a destructive or expensive command. A successful selector command with zero intended resources is not a completed validation.
units.transfer: Construct and inspect a reproducible selection against an explicit baseline. Explain which dependencies and tests are included and which data changes are outside the comparison. The later CI lessons connect that selection to real execution and deferral.

units.title: Documentation, catalogs, exposures and ownership
units.outcome: Build documentation that joins observed structure with authored meaning and ownership.
units.theory:
Documentation has both structural and semantic parts. A database catalog can identify a column's physical type, while a project description explains what the value means. Neither substitutes for the other. A field named total needs a grain, unit, time window and inclusion policy before a consumer can interpret it reliably.

The first case generates real dbt documentation artifacts after building a mart. The catalog records the observed database column, and the manifest records a declared exposure depending on that mart. An exposure represents a downstream use such as a dashboard or application. It improves lineage and ownership visibility, but it does not prove that an external consumer is currently healthy or actually using the declared version.

The second case demonstrates a structurally documented but semantically undescribed model. Its integer type is available, yet its description is empty. A documentation build can therefore succeed while important meaning remains absent. Treat generated artifacts as a foundation for review, not an automatic substitute for authored definitions.
units.syntax: docs generate inspects the built project and writes catalog.json alongside manifest.json. Model and column descriptions live in schema metadata. An exposure names its type, owner and ref-based dependencies. The classroom inspects these JSON artifacts locally; it does not start a separate docs web server or claim that arbitrary generated HTML is a trusted worker result.

worked.title: Connect physical and declared information
worked.explanation: The first case checks a total column in the catalog and the exposure's dependency in the manifest. It combines observed database structure with declared project meaning without confusing the two.
worked.expected: The catalog contains total and the decision-report exposure depends on mart.

worked.title: Detect missing semantics
worked.explanation: The second project builds and documents a model with no authored description. The program verifies that its physical INTEGER type is known while its description is empty.
worked.expected: The type is available, but the business description is missing.

exercises.title: Write a complete definition
exercises.task: Describe total with its grain, units and inclusion rule.
exercises.check: A reader can interpret the quantity without guessing.
exercises.hint: A column name alone is insufficient.
exercises.answer: State which records contribute, the grouping key, time boundary and unit. Keep the definition aligned with the model and tests.

exercises.title: Add a downstream consumer
exercises.task: Declare a second exposure with its owner and dependency.
exercises.check: The new edge appears in the manifest.
exercises.hint: Use ref-based lineage.
exercises.answer: The exposure is a maintained declaration. Validate actual consumer behavior separately and update ownership when responsibility changes.

exercises.title: Inspect physical type
exercises.task: Read the catalog's type for a column.
exercises.check: It matches the built database representation.
exercises.hint: Compilation alone does not create the catalog observation.
exercises.answer: Generate docs against the intended materialized state and retain its invocation/source context. A stale catalog can describe an older deployment.

exercises.title: Find an undocumented field
exercises.task: Create a model column without a description.
exercises.check: The documentation gap remains visible.
exercises.hint: Success of docs generate is not prose completeness.
exercises.answer: Add a semantic review gate appropriate to the project. Avoid automatically filling descriptions with generic repeated text.

exercises.title: Separate lineage from execution
exercises.task: Explain what an exposure cannot establish.
exercises.check: It cannot prove the external dashboard ran successfully.
exercises.hint: Declared relationships differ from runtime observations.
exercises.answer: Combine lineage with actual deployment and service evidence when making operational claims. Keep those evidence sources separately identifiable.

exercises.title: Export a compact review record
exercises.task: Select useful metadata from the generated artifacts.
exercises.check: The record contains meaning, ownership and dependency identifiers.
exercises.hint: Do not dump an entire large manifest into a user message.
exercises.answer: Keep a bounded summary with links or hashes identifying the underlying artifacts. The full files remain the detailed evidence in a durable project.

units.diagnosis: A missing catalog node may mean the model was not materialized or the wrong environment was inspected. An empty description is an authored-content gap. An exposure pointing to the wrong model is a lineage defect even if the database query succeeds. Diagnose these separately.
units.transfer: Build documentation that joins observed structure with authored meaning and ownership. Review a consumer's dependency and record which claims are declarations versus runtime evidence. This creates a useful handoff for analysts, data scientists and operators.

units.title: Publication gates after materialization
units.outcome: Separate candidate computation from accepted publication.
units.theory:
Materialization and publication are different actions. A model relation may exist even when later tests fail. If consumers must not see invalid data, they need an accepted-output boundary that is updated only after the required evidence passes. A successful SQL statement is insufficient for that decision.

The example builds a candidate relation with key tests and publishes a small JSON output only when the complete invocation and relevant statuses pass. The bad fixture still materializes two rows, but no published file is created. The program checks both facts so it cannot confuse detection with transactional rollback.

This is a local publication gate, not a distributed transaction across a warehouse and an object store. A real deployment needs atomic pointer or version selection, ownership, retry behavior and recovery after uncertain outcomes. The lesson establishes the decision rule and evidence boundary that those mechanisms must implement.
units.syntax: Check result.success and the relevant run_results statuses before writing the accepted output. Keep the candidate relation separate from the consumer-facing artifact. A publication receipt should identify the data, schema, source version and checks that justified acceptance. A stale successful artifact must not qualify a new candidate.

worked.title: Publish an accepted candidate
worked.explanation: The valid two-row fixture passes both key conditions and produces a JSON artifact. The program confirms that the artifact exists only after successful evidence is available.
worked.expected: Two candidate rows are present and publication is true.

worked.title: Keep a failed candidate out of the accepted boundary
worked.explanation: The duplicate-key fixture causes a failed test. The database relation still exists, but the publication step is skipped. This is the intended failure policy, not a missing output bug.
worked.expected: Two candidate rows exist, but publication is false.

exercises.title: Change the failure condition
exercises.task: Add a domain test that rejects negative amounts.
exercises.check: The candidate can be blocked by a meaningful semantic failure.
exercises.hint: Key validity is only one dimension.
exercises.answer: Define the condition and verify a designed negative fixture. Do not treat every possible warning as equivalent to an accepted result.

exercises.title: Inspect candidate state
exercises.task: Query the bad relation after failure.
exercises.check: Its materialized rows are still observable.
exercises.hint: Tests may occur after model creation.
exercises.answer: Use this observation to design consumer isolation. Hiding an error message does not remove invalid data from a relation.

exercises.title: Retain an accepted version
exercises.task: Keep a prior valid artifact while a new candidate fails.
exercises.check: The accepted version remains identifiable.
exercises.hint: Separate candidate and accepted paths.
exercises.answer: A consumer should follow a declared accepted version or pointer, not whichever file was most recently written.

exercises.title: Handle an uncertain write
exercises.task: Describe a publication timeout after the write may have occurred.
exercises.check: The response reconciles identity before retrying.
exercises.hint: An unknown outcome is not a confirmed failure.
exercises.answer: Read the intended publication identifier or hash and determine whether it exists. Blind retries can duplicate side effects in less idempotent systems.

exercises.title: Record the evidence
exercises.task: Add a compact receipt beside the accepted data.
exercises.check: It identifies source, checks and data identity.
exercises.hint: A file timestamp is not enough.
exercises.answer: Retain input and model versions, schema/grain, executed test outcomes and output identity. Keep provenance and semantic quality as distinct claims.

exercises.title: Test a stale artifact
exercises.task: Change source data but reuse an old successful run_results file.
exercises.check: A reviewed gate rejects the mismatched evidence.
exercises.hint: Bind evidence to the current candidate.
exercises.answer: Use invocation and source/data identities. A successful result from a different run cannot justify publication of changed data.

units.diagnosis: If invalid data appears despite a failed build, inspect the consumer-facing boundary. If publication is missing after success, check the exact selected statuses and artifact path. Keep failures visible and reconcile uncertain outcomes before retrying. A gate that simply ignores failed tests is not recovery.
units.transfer: Separate candidate computation from accepted publication. Demonstrate both paths and retain a source-bound decision record. Extend the mechanism to an atomic version pointer and a tested recovery plan in a durable owned environment.
